PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 3

Shapes & Patterns

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 3Subjects Shapes & patterns

Twelve shape cards, printable shape sheets to solve and a house full of shapes waiting to be found. This class follows Numbers & Counting on the preschool path — same calm pacing, now with circles, stars and simple patterns.

Two shapes are a fine first day. Start with the ones your child will spot around the house — circle and star are the classics — and let the rest of the set wait its turn.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, little one on the lap or wandering the room — both work.
TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Four little steps, in any order that suits you: a welcome from your teacher, the shape cards, solving the shape sheets together, an off-screen hunt, and a warm goodbye. Stop after any step — that is a complete class, and there is never a score at the end.

  1. 1 Teacher welcome
  2. 2 Learn shapes
  3. 3 Solve the sheets
  4. 4 Take it off screen
  5. 5 Class complete
TEACHER WELCOME

“Hello, my friend — and hello to you, grown-up helper! Today we’re playing with shapes. Start with the ones your child already loves — circles and stars are old friends — and let the rest introduce themselves.”

— Your Kiddo School teacher

Begin the class ↓First stop: the shape cards.
LEARN SHAPES

Twelve shapes, from circle to octagon.

Every card shows one big, friendly shape with its name underneath. Use the arrows to wander through them in order — or simply scroll. Name each shape, trace it in the air with one big finger movement, and stop whenever the wiggles start.

Card 1 of 12
Or simply scroll: all 12 cards are below.
SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the shape sheets together.

The twelve shape cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and named, they are the class’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twelve, two to a page. Cut them out together, naming each shape as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Name the shape

    Hold up a card and name the shape, then count its sides together — one, two, three. Sides and names grow up side by side.

  3. 03

    Hunt the twins

    Find each shape’s real twin in the room: the clock is a circle, the book is a rectangle. One real twin per shape is plenty.

  4. 04

    Trace the edge

    Trace around each card’s edge with one finger, then a crayon. On screen, the card page’s Write & Color layer does the same job.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Shapes that live in your house.

Shape names stick best away from the screen, in short playful hunts with real things. Pick one of these — two minutes is plenty — and follow your child’s lead.

Plate shapes

  • At snack time, look at the food: round cucumber slices, square crackers, oval eggs.
  • Name each shape as you serve it — “a circle of cucumber for you!”

Doors and windows

  • Wander one room together and find rectangles: the door, a book, a window.
  • Tap each one gently and say “rectangle” — the shape your child touches all day, finally with a name.

Shapes on a walk

  • Outside, wheels are circles, signs can be octagons, and the sun is a circle in the sky.
  • One or two shapes per outing is exactly right; the world will still be there tomorrow.

Playdough shapes

  • Roll a ball (circle!), squash it into an egg (oval!), stretch it long (rectangle!).
  • Shapes your hands have made are shapes your memory keeps.

Make a pattern together

  • Line up blocks, buttons or pasta: circle, square, circle, square... and ask what comes next.
  • Let your child build the pattern and YOU be the one who guesses — getting it wrong on purpose is the fun part.

Stay close, keep it playful and stop while it is still fun. There is nothing to finish here.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

At three, shape play is naming and noticing, not geometry lessons: a “diamond” that is really a kite, an “oval” that is really an egg — all of it is exactly on track. The pattern games here are rhythm games in disguise; saying the pattern out loud matters more than tapping the right tile. Everything gives calm feedback with no scores, and the pattern tiles are drawn by the page itself, so the game never depends on a picture that might not load.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Sit together for the card viewing, and let your child do the tapping in the games — even when the answer looks obvious to you. Naming a shape and tracing it in the air at the same time is twice as sticky as either one alone.

Keep shape words casual and plentiful: “round plate”, “square window”, “that long rectangle of a rug”. The shapes do not need a quiz — they need to show up in ordinary chat until they feel like old friends.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class was a circle, a star and a snack, today’s class was a success.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Circle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The circle starts the class because it is the shape a child meets first and names soonest — wheels before breakfast, plates at every meal. This lesson gives the roundness a rule (no corners anywhere), a movement (rolling), and a house-wide hunt that turns every room into practice.

    What is this?

    A circle is a flat shape whose edge curves the whole way round — no corners, no straight sides, no beginning and no end. Walk your finger along it and you arrive back where you started. On the card it is one big red circle with a shiny highlight, and it is the shape of things that roll: balls, wheels and coins.

    What does it mean?

    Corner-free is the meaning children feel first: nothing sticks out, nothing pokes, nothing stops the finger. That smoothness is also the physics — round things roll because nothing catches. A child who traces the edge once and then rolls a ball has met both halves of the idea: the look of a circle and the reason wheels work.

    What does the child need to know?

    Three ideas carry the lesson: a circle is round all the way round with no corners at all, round things roll because nothing sticks out, and circles are everywhere once the word is awake. Keep a ball nearby — the card shows the shape, the ball proves the rule.

    Why this matters

    Shape names are sorting tools: a child who can pull all the round things out of a mixed pile is classifying, the same thinking that later sorts letters from numbers and animals from vehicles. The circle is the kindest place to start, because the household supplies endless examples and the rule is only one word long: round.

    What it teaches

    Shape vocabulary, smooth edge-tracing for fine motor control, rolling and catching for gross motor work, visual matching (card circle to plate, clock face, wheel), and the first idea that shapes are rules a thing either follows or does not.

    Words to learn

    circleroundrollcorneredgeball

    Say this to your child

    ““Circle! Round and round and round — no corners anywhere, not even one. Run your finger all the way around the edge... feel how it never stops turning? That is what a circle is. Now roll the ball — see, nothing catches! Circles roll. Let us find three more circles in this room!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and say circle, then walk one finger all the way around the edge — round and round, never lifting, never turning a corner.
    2. Ask what is missing: how many corners can your child find? Zero is the answer, and zero is a fun number to shout.
    3. Roll a ball across the floor and watch why: nothing sticks out, so nothing catches. Say the rule — circles roll.
    4. Hunt the house for circles: plates, clock faces, buttons, toy wheels. Tap each one and say the word together.
    5. Finish with the air-trace: one big circle drawn with a whole arm in the air, while saying the word once, slowly.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: one big red circle with a shiny highlight, and the word circle underneath. Where does the shine sit — near the top or off to the side? Does the red edge ever turn a corner, or does it curve the whole way round? Which circle at home matches it best?

    Ask your child

    “How many corners does a circle have?” “Which things in the kitchen are circles?” “Why do wheels work — what shape are they?” “Can you draw a circle in the air?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might announce circle at every plate, coin and wheel in sight, demand a rolling race down the hallway, or air-trace the shape in mid-air while telling a story — a shape owned by the body gets drawn on everything, including the air.

    Out in the real world

    Circles repeat all day: the round kitchen table, the clock, the buttons on a cardigan, the wheels of the pram, the plate at every meal. Name them as you pass — a household full of circles is a household full of free rehearsals, and the word costs nothing at the till.

    Try it together

    The rolling race: sit facing your child and roll a ball back and forth, announcing circle every time it leaves your hands. Then graduate to the floor hunt — three round things brought to the rug and lined up beside the card. Rolling is the physics; the naming is the lesson.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “How many corners does a circle have? What does a circle do that a square cannot? Show me round with your finger.” Zero, roll and a smooth air-trace — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If everything remotely round gets called circle, enjoy the enthusiasm — precision arrives with repetition, not correction. If an oval gets claimed as a circle, answer honestly and lightly: “almost — a circle is round the whole way, that one got stretched,” and let the oval card finish the thought later.

    This lesson pairs with the Circle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Square — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The square is the shape children count on first, because everything about it is fair: four sides the same, four corners the same, no surprises. This lesson turns that fairness into a ritual — count the sides, count the corners, find the shape — and then hands over the blocks, because squares are the shape that builds.

    What is this?

    A square has four straight sides, all matching in length, and four corners, all matching in size. That equality is its whole character: nothing longer, nothing shorter, nothing leaning. On the card it is one big yellow square with a shiny highlight and the word square underneath — and in your kitchen it is crackers, window panes and the side of a box.

    What does it mean?

    Fairness is the meaning: same, same, same, same. A child who counts four sides and finds them all equal has met equality in a form they can hold — no arguments, no almosts. That tidy certainty is why squares are the shape of tiles, crackers and building blocks: sameness fits together, and children feel it the moment two blocks stack flush.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the count — four sides, four corners, each side matching the next — and the habit of checking by tracing. One idea to hold loosely and kindly: a square tilted on its corner is still a square. Turn a cracker slowly in the air to prove it, then hand the cracker over.

    Why this matters

    Counting sides and corners is geometry’s first procedure — a rule you can check with one finger. It is also measuring in disguise: same-length sides are the seed of the ruler idea. A child who traces edges now is doing the hand-work that later holds a pencil steady and reads a number line.

    What it teaches

    Counting with one-to-one pointing, straight-edge tracing, shape-rule language (sides, corners, equal, straight), rotation awareness through the tilt test, and construction thinking — blocks stack because their faces are square, and the tower proves it.

    Words to learn

    squarefoursidescornersequalstraight

    Say this to your child

    ““Square! Count with me — one, two, three, four sides. Every side the same! And four corners, one at every stop. Now watch the cracker turn... round and round... still a square! Turning cannot trick a square. Now let us go find four-sided things — and build a tower while we are at it!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and count the sides aloud, one slow finger trip: one, two, three, four — all the same length.
    2. Count the corners the same way: four corners, one at every stop, each one a proper pointy pause.
    3. The tilt test: hold a cracker square and rotate it slowly — still four sides? Still a square? Let your child discover that turning cannot change a shape.
    4. Build together: stack blocks into a tower and notice which faces make it steady — flat and square stack well; round rolls away.
    5. Hunt for squares around the room — window panes, cushions, book covers — and trace each one’s four sides with a fingertip.

    Look closer at the picture

    Study the card: one big yellow square with a shiny highlight and the word square below. How many sides can your child count around it? Where does the highlight sit? Do all four sides look the same length, or is one stretching longer than the rest?

    Ask your child

    “How many sides has a square? How many corners?” “Is a tilted square still a square?” “What can you find with four matching sides?” “Which stacks better — blocks or balls — and why?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might count corners on everything from biscuits to light switches, report every window in the house, or insist crackers be served point-first — a shape with a count gets counted, and the counting is the point.

    Out in the real world

    Squares all over the house: window panes, crackers, sticky notes, floor tiles, the waffle iron, the side of the cereal box. Each one is a four-sided rehearsal waiting to be tapped — and four is a small enough number that the whole count fits in one finger trip.

    Try it together

    Square builders: challenge your child to build the tallest tower that stands still, using only blocks with flat, square faces — then roll a ball against it and discuss why the tower wins and the ball loses. Stacking is geometry the hands can feel, and the crash at the end is the bell for round two.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “How many sides? How many corners? Is a tilted square still a square?” Four, four and a confident yes — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If your child calls long rectangles squares, skip the correction and set the two cards side by side: “which one got stretched?” The comparison does the teaching, and your child gets to be the one who spots it. Keep a box of square crackers on standby — the tastiest shape rule in the house.

    This lesson pairs with the Square flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Triangle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The triangle is the shape children meet pointing at them — roofs, mountains, pizza slices, the classic rocket. This lesson teaches its one rule (three straight sides, three corners), builds one out of fingers, and finishes at lunch, where a grown-up knife turns an ordinary sandwich into three-sided practice.

    What is this?

    A triangle has three straight sides and three corners — that is the whole rule, and it covers every triangle there is, from wide and squat to long and skinny. On the card it is one big green triangle with a shiny highlight and the word triangle underneath. In the world it is roofs, ramps, sails and slices.

    What does it mean?

    One rule, many shapes: wide triangles, skinny triangles, upside-down triangles — all three-sided, all legal. That is a genuinely big idea wearing a small shape. A child who accepts a long skinny triangle as a real one has started to classify by rule instead of by picture, which is the beginning of all category thinking.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the count — three sides, three corners — and the wide permission inside the rule: skinny counts, tilted counts, any three straight sides make one. The finger-triangle below gives the shape a body your child can carry everywhere, and the sandwich gives it a taste.

    Why this matters

    Rule-based classification is the quiet engine of early learning: letters, numbers, animals and shapes all sort this way. The triangle is the friendliest trainer because the rule is tiny, the examples are delicious, and the word itself — tri-angle — contains its own clue, three, if anyone cares to hear it.

    What it teaches

    Counting to three with pointing, rule-based classification, finger positioning and hand strength in the finger-triangle, snack-time patience while the grown-up cuts, and the drawing connection — triangles become roofs and mountains on every page from now on.

    Words to learn

    trianglethreesidespointycornerroof

    Say this to your child

    ““Triangle! Three sides — one, two, three — and three pointy corners. Make one with your fingers: thumbs together, pointer across... you made a triangle! Turn it sideways — still three sides, still a triangle. Now — who wants their sandwich cut into triangles today?””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace the three sides slowly, counting as you go: one, two, three.
    2. Build the finger-triangle: two thumbs tip to tip and one pointer stretched across — a shape your child can make anywhere, any time.
    3. Hunt triangles in picture books — roofs, mountains, hats, sails — and tap each one as it is found.
    4. The tilt-and-flip test: turn the card on its side — still three sides? Then it is still a triangle.
    5. Lunch finale: a grown-up cuts a sandwich corner to corner — two triangles! Count the sides of yours before the first bite.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: one big green triangle with a shiny highlight and the word triangle underneath. How many corners can your child point to? Where does the shine sit? Are the three sides matching, or does one stretch longer than the other two?

    Ask your child

    “How many sides does a triangle have? How many corners?” “Is a long skinny triangle still a triangle?” “Where did we find triangles today?” “What happens to a square if you cut it corner to corner?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might flash finger-triangles at random moments, spot roofs from the car window, or request triangle sandwiches by name — a shape that lives in the fingers gets made everywhere, and every making is a repetition.

    Out in the real world

    Triangles on every walk and every plate: rooftops, road signs, slices of pizza and toast, the mountain in a storybook. The rule is short enough to repeat at each sighting — three straight sides — and the sightings are constant, which is what makes the word stick.

    Try it together

    Triangle snacks: a grown-up cuts toast or cheese into triangles of different sizes — wide, skinny, tiny — and your child sorts and names them all before eating. Every one of them is a real triangle, which is the whole rule, served for lunch.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “How many sides? Make a triangle with your fingers. Is a skinny one still a triangle?” Three, the finger shape and a yes — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Do not police imperfect drawings — three-ish sides at three years old is the idea arriving, and hand strength grows through drawing, not correction. If your child rejects the long word, break it into claps: tri-an-gle, three claps for three sides, and let the rhythm carry the word home.

    This lesson pairs with the Triangle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Rectangle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The rectangle is the shape your child has been touching all day without knowing its name — the door, the book, the table, the screen. This lesson names it through its own best trick: it is a square that got stretched. Two sides stay short, two grow long, and suddenly half the house has a name.

    What is this?

    A rectangle has four straight sides and four corners, like a square — but its sides are not all matching: two are long and two are short. On the card it is one big green rectangle, stretched long, with the word rectangle underneath. Stretch a square and you have made one; that story is the lesson.

    What does it mean?

    The stretch is the idea. Same four corners, same four sides — but pulled, so long sides appear where equals used to be. A child who acts the stretch with their own hands (square arms... pull... rectangle!) has learned that shapes relate to each other: one can become another by growing. That is pre-geometry, met with the whole body.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the four-and-four count they already own from the square, plus the new fact: on a rectangle, two sides stretch. The house is the practice hall — doors, drawers, books, biscuit tins and towels all wear the shape, and the door itself is a rectangle your child can stand inside.

    Why this matters

    Comparing side lengths is measuring’s first step: longer and shorter are the words a ruler will one day put numbers to. The rectangle also teaches transfer — a rule learned on squares stretches to fit a new shape — and children who watch one idea flex like that learn that rules can be trusted to travel.

    What it teaches

    Length comparison (long versus short sides), straight-edge tracing, transfer of a known rule to a new shape, spatial language (stretched, wide, long), and the door-and-book naming habit that rehearses the word daily without any extra work.

    Words to learn

    rectanglelongshortstretchsidesdoor

    Say this to your child

    ““Rectangle! Like a square, but stretched — looong this way. Four sides, four corners, but two of them grew. Look — the door is a rectangle, the book is a rectangle, the table is a rectangle! The whole house is wearing this shape. Can you stretch your arms out like a rectangle?””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace all four sides, then ask which two are the long ones — let your child find the stretch.
    2. Say the story: a rectangle is a square that got stretched — pull your hands slowly apart as you say it.
    3. Compare side by side: set the rectangle card next to the square card. Same corners? Same sides? What changed?
    4. The door test: walk to a door and trace its edges — a rectangle your child can stand inside!
    5. Book hunt: how many rectangles live on one bookshelf? Spines, covers, drawers — count a few, then let the counting wander.

    Look closer at the picture

    On the card: one big green rectangle, stretched long, with the word rectangle underneath. Which sides look long, and which look short? Which way does the stretch run — up and down, or across? Can your child trace all four sides without lifting a finger?

    Ask your child

    “Which two sides of a rectangle are long?” “Is a door a rectangle?” “What did the square do to become a rectangle?” “How many rectangles can you find in this room?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might stretch their arms at every mention of the word, call out doors and books across the house, or discover that the fridge is a rectangle and report it like news — a shape with a stretch story gets retold with gestures, every time.

    Out in the real world

    Rectangles run the household: doors, books, tables, screens, drawers, the bath towel, the rug. Name the big ones as you pass — the front door alone rehearses the word twice a day, and it never once needs a flashcard to do it.

    Try it together

    Hand-measuring: how many hands long is the kitchen table? Place your child’s hand at one end, yours next to it, and count together — three hands, four hands. Any rectangle becomes measurable, and your child has just discovered why people invented measuring, at snack-table scale.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What did a square do to become a rectangle? How many corners? Name a rectangle you can stand inside.” Stretched, four, the door — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If the square-versus-rectangle border gets blurry, answer simply and honestly: matching sides make a square, two long and two short make a rectangle, and looking carefully is how you tell. Do not rush to say a square is also a rectangle — that truth keeps beautifully for age six.

    This lesson pairs with the Rectangle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Oval — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The oval arrives holding hands with the circle, because it is the circle with a story: something stretched it. Eggs, balloons, spoons — the shape of a gentle pull. This lesson lets your child do the stretching, in playdough first and in words second, until the difference between round and almost-round is something their hands already know.

    What is this?

    An oval is like a circle that has been stretched — longer one way, still smooth and corner-free, with no straight sides anywhere. On the card it is one big purple oval, stretched like a balloon, with the word oval underneath. Eggs are ovals. So are balloons, plums and the bowl of a spoon.

    What does it mean?

    Near-twins teach precision. Circle and oval are so close that telling them apart is a genuine act of looking — round the whole way, or pulled? A child who holds both ideas at once, without collapsing them into one, is doing fine visual work: the same careful seeing that later tells b from d and p from q.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the stretch story — round became long — and a feel for the in-between: an oval is not a circle and not a rectangle; it is its own shape. The playdough game makes the whole journey physical: ball, then pull, then oval, then roll it back.

    Why this matters

    Shape transformation is big mathematical weather: one thing becoming another by stretching is the idea behind triangles into parallelograms and squares into boxes, years from now. Meeting it at three, with playdough and an egg, plants the idea where the hands can reach it again.

    What it teaches

    Shape-transformation thinking, comparison language (round, stretched, longer), fine motor work in pinching and rolling playdough, observation of natural ovals (eggs, plums, leaves), and the flexibility to hold two near-twin shapes apart without merging them.

    Words to learn

    ovaleggstretchroundsmoothballoon

    Say this to your child

    ““Oval! A circle that got stretched — see? Long this way, smooth all the way round, no corners at all. Roll the playdough... now stretch it gently... it became an oval! Just like an egg. Can you make your hands into a big oval? Round... and stretch!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace the outline — smooth, no corners, but longer one way.
    2. Tell the story: a circle got stretched — pull your hands gently apart as you say it.
    3. The playdough proof: roll a ball, then stretch it slowly — round... round... oval! Let your child do the pulling.
    4. The egg check: hold a real egg — which way does it curve? Turn it slowly: longer one way, smooth all round.
    5. The balloon connection: a grown-up blows up a balloon part-way and holds it out — an oval in the hand. Let more air in and watch it grow longer still.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card holds one big purple oval, stretched like a balloon, with the word oval underneath. Which way does it stretch — up, down or sideways? Trace the edge with your child: any corners anywhere, or smooth the whole way round? Does it look more like an egg or a balloon?

    Ask your child

    “What did we do to the circle to make an oval?” “Is an egg a circle or an oval?” “Can you stretch your playdough ball into an oval?” “What else is oval in the kitchen?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might stretch their hands into ovals at every egg, inspect balloons like a quality inspector, or roll-and-stretch playdough on a loop — ball, oval, ball, oval — until the two words live in their fingers instead of their ears.

    Out in the real world

    Ovals in the fridge and the toy box: eggs, plums, grapes, balloons, spoon bowls, some bathroom mirrors, the footprint in the sand. Each one is a stretched-circle sighting, and sightings at breakfast count double because the egg is there and so is the appetite.

    Try it together

    The playdough shape machine: roll a ball and call circle — then call oval, and your child stretches it; call circle again, and they roll it back round. Switch the calls faster and faster until their hands know both words by heart. Shape rules are easiest to learn when the hands do the editing.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “How do you make an oval from a circle? Is an egg round or oval? Show me oval with your hands.” Stretch, oval and the pull-apart gesture — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Circle-versus-oval confusion is completely normal — they are near-twins, and near-twins take time. Compare side by side rather than correcting: the circle card and the oval card together, one finger on each edge. The day your child says “this one got stretched” is the day the lesson landed for good.

    This lesson pairs with the Oval flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Star — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The star is usually the shape a child already owns — stickers, reward charts, drawings on the fridge — which makes this the class’s confidence card. This lesson turns fame into precision: a star is five points, here is how to count them, and tonight the sky might just hand over the real thing.

    What is this?

    A star has five points shooting out from a middle — a shape that refuses to sit still the way circles and squares do; it sparkles. On the card it is one big yellow star with five points and the word star underneath. In life, stars live on drawings, decorations and, after dark, much higher up.

    What does it mean?

    The points are the whole identity: count them and you hold the shape. That makes the star a counting shape — five is not decoration, it is the definition — and counting five narrow tips takes more finger control than counting four fat sides. The word arrives already famous; the count is what turns fame into ownership.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the count — one to five, one point per finger — and the drawing bug: stars get drawn everywhere once learned, on every paper and in every margin. The night-sky visit gives the word its most magical rehearsal, and it is free every clear evening.

    Why this matters

    Pointing at five skinny targets is sneaky fine-motor and one-to-one counting practice — the pointer must land precisely, stop and move on. And the star carries a bonus no other shape has: it exists overhead, real and enormous, which turns bedtime into a vocabulary event.

    What it teaches

    One-to-one counting to five, pointing accuracy on narrow targets, air-drawing coordination, shape confidence from a familiar favourite, and the bedtime ritual that attaches vocabulary to wonder — the strongest glue early learning has.

    Words to learn

    starfivepointssparkleskycount

    Say this to your child

    ““Star! Count the points with me — one, two, three, four, five! Five sparkly points. Now look at your hand — five fingers! A hand and a star are the same number. Draw one in the air... up, down, across, zig-zag! And tonight, we will look out of the window for a real one, far away in the sky.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and count the points together, slowly: one, two, three, four, five.
    2. Five fingers, five points: hold up a hand and match finger to point — a hand and a star are the same count.
    3. Draw stars in the air with one big zig-zag arm movement, then on paper with a crayon — wobbly stars count double.
    4. Sticker round: any star stickers in the house? Hand them out and count the points on each one.
    5. Tonight, look out of the window for the first star. If the sky cooperates, your child meets the original.

    Look closer at the picture

    On the card: one big yellow star with five points, and the word star underneath. Can your child touch each point in turn? Is there one point at the very top? Are all five the same size, or does one shoot out longer than the rest?

    Ask your child

    “How many points does a star have? How many fingers do you have — the same number?” “Can you draw a star in the air?” “Where will the first star be tonight?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might draw stars on every available surface, hold up a five-finger star at dinner, or demand the window at dusk — a shape this famous gets produced, counted and celebrated, usually all before breakfast.

    Out in the real world

    Stars fill childhood: stickers, reward charts, wrapping paper, flags, and the actual night sky. Each drawing is a five-point rehearsal, and the sky adds the once-a-day magic round — the only vocabulary review that comes with a wish attached.

    Try it together

    Star jumps: five points, five jumps — jump and count one to five, then freeze into a star shape with arms and legs wide. Repeat until the giggles win. Counting and shape in one game, and the freeze at the end is a proper star, made of one delighted child.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “How many points? Show me five. Draw a star in the air.” Five, the hand and a zig-zag — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Accept wobbly stars — the count matters more than the symmetry, and symmetry arrives with practice. If bedtime star-spotting becomes a ritual, protect it: the reward for a shape lesson should occasionally be the actual night sky, and children who look up once tend to keep looking.

    This lesson pairs with the Star flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Heart — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The heart is the shape children meet attached to affection — on cards, on drawings, on the family noticeboard — and this lesson keeps that warmth. Two bumps on top, one point at the bottom, and a job no other shape has: it means I love you, which is why children learn it early and keep it forever.

    What is this?

    A heart has two round bumps on top and one point at the bottom — a shape made of curves that meets itself in a single point. On the card it is one big red heart with a shiny highlight and the word heart underneath. In life it appears on cards, drawings, biscuits and valentines of every size.

    What does it mean?

    The heart is the class’s first symbol: a shape that means something beyond its own outline. A circle is a circle, but a heart says love — and children absorb symbols early when the symbol carries feeling. Drawing one for a real person turns geometry into a gift, which is why this lesson ends at someone’s door.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the two-part description — round on top, pointy at the bottom — and the drawing practice that puts it in the hand. Keep the feeling-word too: hearts get given away, and giving them is the point. The folded-paper trick below rescues any drawing that goes wrong.

    Why this matters

    Symbol reading starts here: a mark that stands for a feeling is the same leap as a letter standing for a sound. Children who draw hearts for people they love are practising representation — marks that mean — in the warmest possible register, years before reading begins.

    What it teaches

    Two-part shape description (round, pointy), drawing and crayon control, emotional vocabulary alongside shape vocabulary, giving and delivering as social practice, and the pride of making something that matters to someone else.

    Words to learn

    heartloveroundpointycardgive

    Say this to your child

    ““Heart! Two round bumps on top... and one point at the bottom. A heart means I love you — that is its job. Let us draw one: bump, bump, down to the point. Now — who should we give our heart to? Granny? Your best friend? Let us make it beautiful and deliver it!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace it: round, round on top... down to one point at the bottom.
    2. Say the description together until it is a chant: two bumps on top, one point below.
    3. Draw one on paper — bumps first, then the point — and let your child color it in.
    4. The giving job: decide together who the heart is for — a grandparent, a friend, the cat — and deliver it.
    5. Spot hearts around the house: cards, books, biscuit cutters, a bag or a t-shirt — hearts hide in plain sight.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: one big red heart with a shiny highlight and the word heart underneath. Where are the two round bumps — top or bottom? Where is the single point? What color did the artist choose for this heart?

    Ask your child

    “What does a heart shape mean in our family?” “Where are the bumps, and where is the point?” “Who would you like to give a heart to?” “Can you find a heart anywhere in this room?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might produce hearts in every drawing for weeks, declare love mid-lesson without warning, or deliver the finished heart with full ceremony — and if the recipient happens to be the cat, the cat will accept, which completes the lesson nicely.

    Out in the real world

    Hearts all year round: birthday cards, biscuits, the pattern on a dress, doodles on a shopping list. Each sighting is a two-part description waiting to happen — bumps on top, point below — and each giving season is a chance to draw another one for a real person.

    Try it together

    The heart delivery service: your child draws and colors hearts — one per person they love — then delivers them around the house, or posts them to faraway people with a grown-up’s help. Each heart gets traced and described as it is made: bumps on top, point below. Shape practice wearing kindness.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “Where are the bumps and where is the point? What does a heart mean? Who got your heart today?” Top and bottom, love and a name — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If the heart-drawing frustrates, fold a paper in half, draw half a heart along the fold and cut — a perfect heart every time, and a magic trick worth the fold. Expect hearts to keep arriving in drawings for months: that is not repetition, that is ownership.

    This lesson pairs with the Heart flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Diamond — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The diamond is the class’s best magic trick: take a square the child already knows, stand it on its corner, and the same shape gets a new name. This lesson performs the trick slowly, draws a kite to prove the shape flies, and goes gem-hunting through drawers, socks and wrapping paper.

    What is this?

    A diamond is a four-sided shape standing on its point — a square turned to balance on one corner, with a point at the top, a point at the bottom and points at each side. On the card it is one big purple diamond standing on its point, with the word diamond underneath. Kites and gems wear this shape.

    What does it mean?

    Turning changes the name: the same four sides, the same four corners, a new word once the corner points up. That is a deep and delightful idea — position can matter as much as shape — and children find it genuinely funny. A shape with two outfits invites flipping, and every flip is a spatial-reasoning rep.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the tilt story — a square standing on its point becomes a diamond — and the four-sides-four-corners count they already own. The kite drawing gives the shape a story with wind in it; the sock-and-paper hunt gives it a habitat in your own drawers.

    Why this matters

    Rotation awareness is spatial reasoning in its purest form: holding one shape in the mind and turning it. Children who play at flipping squares into diamonds are rehearsing the mental rotation that later handles letters — a b is a d having a turn — and maps, and maths, with a kite attached.

    What it teaches

    Rotation and spatial transformation, shape-rule flexibility (same sides, new position), drawing diagonal lines — a genuine pencil-control step — and the treasure-hunting attention that spots small shapes hiding in patterns.

    Words to learn

    diamondkitepointtiltgemsides

    Say this to your child

    ““Diamond! A square that stood up on its pointy corner — look at it balance! Four sides, still. Four corners, still. But now it is a diamond, like a kite in the sky. Let us draw a kite... and then go hunting for tiny diamonds — they hide on socks and paper!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace from the top point all the way round: point, side, point, side, point, side, point, side.
    2. The trick: take the square card and stand it up on one corner — look, a diamond! Turn it back: a square again. Let your child do the flipping.
    3. Draw a kite together: the diamond body, a string, a wavy tail — then let your child color it in.
    4. The gem hunt: look through drawers and patterns for small diamonds — socks, wrapping paper, quilts, a pack of cards.
    5. Air-trace the diamond big: point at the ceiling, down to the floor — a shape that travels.

    Look closer at the picture

    On the card: one big purple diamond standing on its point, with the word diamond underneath. Which point is at the very top? How many corners can your child count? Does the shape look like it is balancing — and on what, exactly?

    Ask your child

    “What did the square do to become a diamond?” “What flies in the sky shaped like a diamond?” “Where did we find diamonds today?” “How many sides does a diamond have?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might flip cards back and forth narrating the transformation, draw kites in every drawing, or report diamond sightings on clothing and wrapping paper with the excitement of a real gemologist.

    Out in the real world

    Diamonds live in pattern-land: sock patterns, quilt squares on their points, wrapping paper, tiles laid corner-up, the kite in the park on a windy day. Small, repeated and hideable, they reward a child who has just learned to look for points.

    Try it together

    Paper kite mission: draw a big diamond, add a string and some ribbon tail bows — each bow a small diamond too, if the paper allows — then take the kite for a run around the garden or the hallway. Flying it is the reward; the diamond was the lesson, drawn and colored before take-off.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What does a square become when it stands on its point? What shape is a kite? How many sides?” Diamond, diamond and four — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Some children get briefly worried that one shape has two names — resolve it by doing the turn together: “square like this, diamond like this — same shape, two outfits.” Names can describe positions too, and that is real geometry, not a trick being played on anyone.

    This lesson pairs with the Diamond flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Crescent — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The crescent is the shape children already dream about: the moon, in its favourite storybook form. This lesson names it through its own best description — a circle with a bite taken out — serves the shape as a banana slice, and ends at the window, where the real moon gets checked: crescent tonight, or round tonight?

    What is this?

    A crescent is a circle with a curved bite taken out of one side, leaving two points and a slim curve between them. On the card it is one big yellow crescent moon with the word crescent underneath. Bananas curve this way, croissants too, and the moon wears the shape for part of every month.

    What does it mean?

    A shape made by taking away: the crescent is what remains when a bite leaves a circle. That is negative space — the first shape your child will meet that is defined by a missing piece — and children adore it, because the bite is a story they can see. Two points, one curve, and an absence doing all the work.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the bite story and the two points — a crescent is the curve between them. The banana slice gives the shape a taste, and the moon check gives it a ritual that repeats all month for free, with the sky running the schedule.

    Why this matters

    Seeing what is missing is observation of a higher order: the eye must hold the whole circle in mind and subtract. That part-whole thinking is the same muscle that later hears cat inside caterpillar and six inside sixteen — and the moon trains it monthly, on schedule, in the night sky.

    What it teaches

    Part-whole thinking (a circle minus a bite), point-spotting at both tips, snack-time fine motor, lunar vocabulary (moon, crescent, round), and the patience of a night-sky ritual that changes over the month and rewards every check-in.

    Words to learn

    crescentmoonbitecurvepointsnight

    Say this to your child

    ““Crescent! The moon’s shape — a round circle with a big sleepy bite taken out. Chomp! See the two pointy tips? The curve between them is the crescent. Now the banana slices — can you find the crescents on your plate? And tonight we check the sky: is the moon a crescent, or has it grown round again?””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace the curve from tip to tip — sleepy and slow, like a yawn.
    2. Tell the story: it is a circle with a bite taken out. Mime the bite — chomp! — and watch the delight land.
    3. The banana version: a grown-up slices a banana, and your child finds the crescent hiding in each round.
    4. Find the two points — the tips of the crescent — and touch each one on the card.
    5. Tonight’s moon check at the window: crescent tonight, or round tonight? Either answer wins — the question is the game.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows one big yellow crescent moon, with the word crescent underneath. Where are the two tips pointing? Is the curve slim or fat? Does the shape look like a circle with a piece missing — can your child say which piece went missing?

    Ask your child

    “What shape is the moon tonight?” “What happened to the circle in a crescent?” “Where are the crescent’s two points?” “What other foods look like crescents?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might mime the bite at every crescent sighting, inspect banana slices like an astronomer, or deliver the nightly moon report from the window — a shape with a story gets retold at bedtime, which is exactly where this one lives.

    Out in the real world

    Crescents at breakfast and bedtime: banana slices, croissants, the moon in storybooks, moon decorations on mobiles and nursery walls. And then the original, hanging in the sky a few nights a month — the only shape card with a live counterpart the child can point at from bed.

    Try it together

    Moon watch: each night this week, look at the moon together and report — crescent, round, or hiding. Draw what you saw on a paper chart by the bed. The moon itself runs the repetition schedule, and by the end of the month your child owns the vocabulary of the sky.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “What shape is a crescent? Where are its two points? What should we check tonight?” The bite, the tips and the moon — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The moon changes shape all month, which can rattle a child who just learned the word — frame the sky as a game that keeps moving: “the moon plays with its shape; we keep score.” Checking together matters more than any single answer, and a wrong guess tonight is a reason to look again tomorrow.

    This lesson pairs with the Crescent flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Pentagon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The pentagon raises the stakes: five sides, five corners, and a word long enough to be an achievement all by itself. Children who say pentagon out loud own something rare — and this lesson earns it with a slow count, a drawing job and a house fit for a very lucky toy.

    What is this?

    A pentagon has five straight sides and five corners — count them and you have the whole rule. On the card it is one big pink pentagon with five straight sides and the word pentagon underneath. It is not a shape your child meets every day, which is exactly what makes saying it feel powerful.

    What does it mean?

    The count jumps to five, and the word is a trophy. Pentagon is a three-syllable mouthful that most adults rarely say, so a three-year-old who says it owns a rare thing — and rare things get repeated. The pride is the pedagogy: a child showing off a long shape word is rehearsing it for free.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the count — five sides, five corners, one slow finger trip around the edge — and the courage of the long word: pen-ta-gon, three claps. The five-sided house drawing turns the count into a gift, and the gift needs a tenant.

    Why this matters

    Counting sides generalizes: shapes can be named by their numbers, which is the whole system — three, four, five, six, eight — hiding behind the names. Meeting the pattern now, with the word as a prize, teaches that new shapes are new counts, not new mysteries.

    What it teaches

    Counting to five on edges, slow-trace finger control, syllable clapping on a three-part word, drawing closed shapes with a target number of sides, and the vocabulary pride of a word most adults rarely say out loud.

    Words to learn

    pentagonfivesidescornershousecount

    Say this to your child

    ““Pentagon! Pen-ta-gon — three claps for this word! Five straight sides: one, two, three, four, five. And five corners, one at every stop. Let us draw a house with five sides... a pentagon house! Who should live in it? Choose your luckiest toy.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and take one slow finger trip around all five sides, counting aloud: one, two, three, four, five.
    2. Clap the word: pen-ta-gon — three claps for three parts. Say it like a cheer.
    3. Draw a five-sided house together — pentagon body first, then a door and windows your child adds.
    4. Count the corners the same way as the sides — five again? Let your child check and report.
    5. Move in a toy: which lucky teddy gets the pentagon house? The drawing is the lesson; the tenant is the reward.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: one big pink pentagon with five straight sides and the word pentagon underneath. Can your child count the sides with one finger? Which side sits at the very top? Are the corners pointy — and how many are there?

    Ask your child

    “How many sides does a pentagon have? Clap the word — how many parts?” “What did we draw with five sides?” “Is a pentagon round anywhere, or all straight?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might announce pentagon at random moments for the pleasure of the sound, clap the word at the dinner table, or assign a beloved toy to the drawn house with full paperwork — a rare word used proudly is a word fully owned.

    Out in the real world

    Pentagons are rare guests in daily life — some street signs, the famous five-sided building, the home-plate shape in baseball pictures — and their rarity is the lesson’s charm. The count and the claps travel; the sightings, when they come, feel like spotting a celebrity.

    Try it together

    Five-side builders: lay five straws or craft sticks on the table and challenge your child to make them into a closed shape with no gaps. Five sides, five corners — when it closes, it is a pentagon, and it deserves a toy inside. Building the count beats counting the build.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “How many sides? Clap the word. What lives in your pentagon house?” Five, three claps and a name — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Five is a big count and wobbles are normal — keep the finger moving and the counting calm; the trip around the shape matters more than perfect pointing. And let the long word be fun: a child who says pentagon at breakfast has already won the morning.

    This lesson pairs with the Pentagon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Hexagon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The hexagon arrives with the best story in the class: it is the shape bees build with. Six sides, six corners, and a fitting-together trick that honeycombs use to hold honey without wasting any space. This lesson counts the six, tells the bee story and builds a real hexagon from coins and pencils.

    What is this?

    A hexagon has six straight sides and six corners. On the card it is one big teal hexagon with six straight sides and the word hexagon underneath. Its famous talent is fitting: hexagons sit side by side with no gaps, which is why honeycombs — and some fences and floor tiles — are built from them.

    What does it mean?

    Fitting is the hexagon’s superpower: some shapes tile a surface snugly and others leave gaps, and the hexagon is the champion of snug. A child who pushes six-sided rooms together and finds no spaces has discovered tessellation — the reason the bee story is true — with their own hands.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the count — six sides, traced slowly — and the bee story, retold at will: bees build with hexagons because the rooms fit together perfectly. The coin game below builds a hexagon-shaped gap out of round coins, which is the kind of magic children retell for weeks.

    Why this matters

    Tessellation is deep spatial maths met through insects: shapes that fit define how tilers, bees and package designers think. And a shape attached to a story sticks — the child who retells “bees build with hexagons” at every opportunity is doing exactly what memory wants.

    What it teaches

    Counting to six on edges, fit-and-tile spatial reasoning, the bee-biology connection, fine motor work in coin placing and tracing, and narrative memory — a shape attached to a story sticks harder than a shape attached to a drill.

    Words to learn

    hexagonsixsidesbeehoneycombfit

    Say this to your child

    ““Hexagon! Six straight sides — one, two, three, four, five, six. And do you know who loves hexagons most? BEES! Bees build with hexagons because the rooms fit together perfectly, no gaps, like a puzzle. Let us do the coin trick and find a hidden hexagon... there it is!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace all six sides slowly, counting together: one to six.
    2. Tell the bee story: bees build their honey houses from hexagons, because six-sided rooms fit together with no gaps.
    3. The coin trick: trace around one coin, then tuck five more coins tightly around it and trace them — the space left in the middle is a hexagon.
    4. Look at honey: if there is a honey jar in the kitchen, check the label or a honeycomb picture together and find the six-sided rooms.
    5. Build it again from craft sticks or straws — six sides, closed, no gaps — and admire it the way a bee would.

    Look closer at the picture

    On the card: one big teal hexagon with six straight sides and the word hexagon underneath. Can your child trace all six sides without stopping? Which side is on top? Do the sides all look the same length, or is one stretching longer?

    Ask your child

    “How many sides does a hexagon have? Who builds with hexagons, and why?” “What happens when hexagons sit next to each other?” “Can we build a hexagon from sticks?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might retell the bee fact to every visitor, count sixes on tiles and fences, or build hexagons from anything straight at hand — a shape with a resident story gets narrated, and the narration is the revision.

    Out in the real world

    Hexagons hide in plain sight: honeycomb patterns on jars and boxes, some floor tiles, the hex heads of nuts and bolts, the patches on a football. Once the bee story is told, every sighting becomes evidence — the child starts finding the shape the insects built their world from.

    Try it together

    The hexagon hive: draw or tape a big honeycomb of touching hexagons on paper or the floor, and let your child fill each room with a toy bee, a pom-pom or a piece of snack cereal — one per room, counted aloud. Fitting things into hexagon rooms is the game the bees invented first.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “How many sides? Who builds with them? What happens when they sit together?” Six, bees and a no-gaps answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If the coin trick flops — small hands and pencils have off days — skip ahead to the stick build: six craft sticks on the table close into a hexagon just as honestly. The bee story carries the lesson even on days when the building refuses.

    This lesson pairs with the Hexagon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · SHAPES & PATTERNS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Octagon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The octagon closes the class with the shape that has a job: eight sides, and a famous red one that tells cars to stop. Children in car seats meet it weekly at junctions, which makes this the set’s most public shape. This lesson counts all eight, honours the stop sign and turns the word into a freeze game.

    What is this?

    An octagon has eight straight sides and eight corners — a big count and a big shape. On the card it is one big orange octagon with eight straight sides and the word octagon underneath. Its famous cousin is the red stop sign: eight sides, telling every car in the land to halt.

    What does it mean?

    A shape can be a signal: the octagon means stop, and every child in a car seat has watched it work. That is symbol reading — a visual form carrying a rule — years before letters do the same job. And eight is the biggest count in the class, so finishing it feels like a graduation.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs the count — eight sides, finished together if the counting runs out of steam — and the stop-sign connection, which turns every walk and drive into a hunt. The freeze game gives the word a whole-body meaning: octagon up, everything stops.

    Why this matters

    Road signs are a child’s first public symbols: shapes that mean things to everyone, everywhere, for free. Learning that the octagon is the stop shape gives a three-year-old a piece of the adult world’s code — and a reason to look out of the window with intent.

    What it teaches

    Counting to eight (with cheerful adult rescue), shape-to-symbol association, whole-body impulse control in the freeze game, street-sign awareness and road-talk at child level, and the long-word pride that closes the whole set.

    Words to learn

    octagoneightsidesstopsignfreeze

    Say this to your child

    ““Octagon! Eight sides — one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight! And this shape has the most famous job of all: the STOP sign is an octagon. Red, eight sides, and every car stops. Now you hold the card — when you raise it, I freeze! Ready? Dance, dance... OCTAGON! Freeze!””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and count all eight sides together, slowly — and if the counting wobbles at six, finish it cheerfully yourself: ...seven, eight!
    2. Tell the job story: somewhere out there is a red octagon that tells cars to STOP. The shape itself is the message.
    3. Play the freeze game: dance until someone holds up the octagon card — then freeze! The card is the stop sign now.
    4. On the next walk or drive, hunt for the real one: red, eight sides, at the corner. Spotting it in the wild is the jackpot.
    5. Close the class: lay out as many of the twelve shape cards as you can and let your child name their favourites — the set is complete, and so is the vocabulary.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the card together: one big orange octagon with eight straight sides and the word octagon underneath. Can your child count the sides — or count a few and let you finish? Which side sits at the top? How many corners does the count reach?

    Ask your child

    “How many sides does an octagon have? What sign is an octagon — and what does it tell cars?” “What happened when the card went up in our game?” “Where might we see one on the road?”

    What your child can say or do

    Your child might freeze dramatically at home whenever a card goes up, count sides on every red sign in sight, or shout octagon from the car seat at junctions — the shape with a job gets reported whenever it reports for duty.

    Out in the real world

    Octagons on the road and around town: stop signs at every corner, octagonal mirrors in driveways, gazebo roofs in picture books, octagonal tables and clocks. Every red eight-sided sign is a sighting, and sightings from the car seat come with built-in ceremony.

    Try it together

    Stop and go, octagon edition: your child dances while you say go, and freezes the instant you hold up the octagon card and call its name. Swap roles so they raise the card too — being the one who says stop is where the word gets its power. Eight sides, one freeze, endless replays.

    Understanding check

    Ask: “How many sides? What does the red octagon tell cars? What did you do when the card came up?” Eight, stop and a frozen statue — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Eight is a stretch at this age, and running out of count around six is normal — model the cheerful finish (...seven, eight!) and let your child chime in on the last side. The stop-sign sighting on a real walk will do more for this word than any drill, so keep the card in your pocket, just in case.

    This lesson pairs with the Octagon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Shapes & Patterns (Preschool).
